genre.label: Genre and how to read it
genre.hint: Once you choose it, questions appear for reading the book according to its genre.

historical-narrative.conflict: What conflict or tension drives the story?
historical-narrative.turn: Where is the turning point, the moment the situation changes?
historical-narrative.resolution: How is it resolved, or what is left open?
historical-narrative.narrator: How does the narrator evaluate what happens: comments, repetitions, silences?
historical-narrative.god: Where does God act in the story, and how does the narrator say so?
historical-narrative.protagonist: Who is the protagonist: a leader or the people?
historical-narrative.sources: What documents, lists or first-person passages does the narrator use, and why?

law.covenant: Which covenant does this law belong to, and to whom was it given?
law.character: What does it show about God's character and what he expects of his people?
law.fulfillment: How does the New Testament take it up in light of Christ?
law.principle: What principle remains when moving from Israel to the church?

poetry.images: What images does it use, and what did they evoke for the first readers?
poetry.tone: What tone dominates: lament, praise, trust, petition?
poetry.shift: Where does the tone or the speaking voice change?

wisdom.observation: What does it observe about life, and how does it ground it in the fear of the Lord?
wisdom.promise: Is it a general observation or a promise? A proverb is not a guarantee.
wisdom.contrast: What contrast does it draw: wise and fool, righteous and wicked?
wisdom.dialogue: How does it converse with the rest of wisdom, such as Job or Ecclesiastes?

prophecy.situation: What historical situation does the prophet address?
prophecy.form: What form does the oracle take: judgment, call to repentance, promise of restoration?
prophecy.covenant: What breach of covenant does it denounce, or what covenant promise does it recall?
prophecy.fulfillment: What was fulfilled in Israel's history, what in Christ, and what is still awaited?

gospel.jesus: What does the scene reveal about who Jesus is?
gospel.response: How do the characters respond: faith, rejection, misunderstanding?
gospel.placement: Why does the evangelist place it here, between what comes before and after?
gospel.parallels: What does it share with the parallel accounts, and how does it differ?

epistle.occasion: What situation in the church prompted the letter?
epistle.argument: How does the argument move: which connectors join it (therefore, because, but)?
epistle.indicative: What has God done, and what is asked of the church?
epistle.whole: How does each part fit the argument of the whole letter?

apocalyptic.symbols: What symbols does it use, and from which Old Testament passages do they come?
apocalyptic.comfort: What comfort or warning does it give readers under pressure?
apocalyptic.sovereignty: What does it affirm about God's rule over history?
apocalyptic.restraint: Which details should not be forced into a timetable?

dialog.title: The framing: passage and purpose
dialog.description: Your reading of the book before seeing the panorama. Write whatever you like: only the book is needed to save.
dialog.noBooks: Choose at least one book to save.
dialog.ezraNehemiah: In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are one book. You can select both.
dialog.scopeRangeLabel: The section in {{book}}, using your Bible's numbering
dialog.scopeOnlyOneBook: A section is chosen with a single book selected.
dialog.scopeError: That section is not recognized in your Bible. Write it like 4:6-23 or 1-6.
dialog.versesNeeded: In this section your Bible's numbering differs from the original text's: write it with verses at the start and the end (chapter:verse).
dialog.readFirst: Before dividing it, read the whole book in one sitting.
dialog.chapterTitles: A one-line title for each chapter
dialog.chapterTitlesHint: Fill in as many as you like.
dialog.droppedTitles: You unselected {{books}}: saving removes the chapter titles you wrote there.
dialog.repetitionsHint: Words, phrases or scenes that recur. Look for them yourself in the text.
dialog.yourReadingHint: Provisional: you will test it against the panorama and against each study. Each field carries the verses that support it. This does not reach the sermon until you review your central idea.
dialog.pastoralHint: This does reach the sermon draft, only to guide the application.
dialog.christTrajectoryHint: How this book leads to Christ: through the history of redemption, promise and fulfillment, figures that anticipate Christ, themes that continue in the New Testament, or by contrast.
dialog.structure: Structure: the movements of the book
dialog.structureHint: Each movement with its section and a short title saying what it is about. With several books, write the book: "Neh 1-7".
dialog.movementError: Check the movements: each one needs a section of your Bible, like 1-6 or 4:6-23.
dialog.needEvidence: Which text in the book shows that it addresses that need?
dialog.needEvidenceHint: The biblical world first: look for the need the text addressed in its first readers that your congregation also has.
dialog.rhythmHint: The schedule gives the dates; the text decides the division into pericopes.
dialog.sundaysError: Write how many Sundays with a number from 1 to {{max}}.

scaffold.wellDone: What it looks like done well

passage.name: Your reading of the book
passage.purpose: Write what you think the book says before dividing it, so you have something to measure your findings against.
passage.wellDone: The book, why you study it, its movements and a one-sentence central idea, written by you.
passage.commonError: Waiting until the studies are done to write it: by then there is no reading left for the text to correct.

sources.name: Sources
sources.purpose: Choose with judgment the works you will use for the whole book: your state of the art, the reasoned list of works you will work with.
sources.wellDone: Approved works of several kinds (commentaries, lexicons, grammars) and the requirements met or accepted on purpose. An approved work can still be «to get».
sources.commonError: Gathering everything in the library without deciding what each work contributes.

division.name: Division into pericopes
division.purpose: Divide the book into pericopes (each unit of the text that is preached whole) following the text's own markers.
division.wellDone: Each pericope with a beginning and an end the text justifies, ordered in a series.
division.commonError: Cutting by chapters or by the number of Sundays instead of by the units of the text.

pericopes.name: Studies by pericope
pericopes.purpose: Study each pericope in depth, in the order of the plan.
pericopes.wellDone: Assembled studies, each noted in your reading: what it confirms, nuances or contradicts.
pericopes.commonError: Opening many studies at once and finishing none.

synthesis.name: Synthesis
synthesis.purpose: Return to your central idea with what the studies said.
synthesis.wellDone: A revised idea, with its reason, that comes from your notes.
synthesis.commonError: Repeating the original idea without looking at what the text nuanced or contradicted.

charge.name: What the course asks for
charge.purpose: Know what the course asks for before writing: the work types, their rubric, method and guide.
charge.wellDone: Each work type with its rubric settled and, where it applies, its style guide.
charge.commonError: Starting the first assignment without knowing which rubric will grade it.

sources.name: Course sources
sources.purpose: Gather the course bibliography in the state of the art, the reasoned list of works you will work with.
sources.wellDone: The required works approved and on hand; the rest chosen for what they bring to each work type.
sources.commonError: Leaving a required work «to get» until the week it is due.

calendar.name: Delivery calendar
calendar.purpose: Keep in view what is due and when.
calendar.wellDone: Each delivery with its work type and date, or the explicit decision to work week by week.
calendar.commonError: Writing down only the next delivery and learning about the following one too late.

works.name: Assignments
works.purpose: Do each assignment with its type, its rules and its sources.
works.wellDone: Assignments assembled before the date and, if the course asks, without repeating sources from the previous one.
works.commonError: Finishing at the last minute and delivering without the review before delivering.

feedback.name: Feedback and learning
feedback.purpose: Learn from what the professor corrects so the next assignment is better.
feedback.wellDone: Each piece of feedback recorded, and each repeated correction decided: moved to your guide or dismissed.
feedback.commonError: Reading the grade and filing the feedback without changing anything in the next assignment.
